activities.anchor: the photograph becomes the accounting equation
activities.caption: file each item — photograph (a moment) or video (a period)?
activities.name: acStoryBuckets

config.prompt: The fruit stall tells two stories. File each item into the right one:

items.label: the till cash on Friday evening
what you sold during the week
the 5 dollars borrowed from your neighbour
what you spent over the week
the unsold fruit on the shelf tonight
what was left over once the week was done

config.why: The photograph becomes the accounting equation (what you have and owe right now); the video becomes the profit calculation (what happened over the period).

activities.caption: pair the master words with their meaning
activities.name: acWordsMatch

config.prompt: Three master words carry the whole subject — match them:

pairs.right: a resource of value the business owns or controls — cash, inventory, machinery
an amount the business owes to outsiders — loans, unpaid supplier bills
the owner's stake — what the business would owe back to the owner
assets minus liabilities — the number profit exists to grow

config.why: Vocabulary first, equation second: the equation is just these three words forced to balance.

activities.anchor: the number that profit exists to grow
activities.caption: find the faulty line — Amina's first week
activities.name: acAminaSpot

config.prompt: One line of this ledger story is wrong — click it:
lines: Amina invests 10,000 dollars: assets +10,000, capital +10,000. The equation holds.
She buys a van for 5,000 with a bank loan: assets +5,000, liabilities +5,000. Holds again.
She repays 2,000 of the loan from cash: liabilities fall to 3,000 and capital falls to 8,000.
config.correction: Repaying the loan reduces assets (cash −2,000) and liabilities (−2,000) equally — capital is untouched at 10,000.
config.why: Loan repayment is a move between asset and liability. Only profit or drawings touch the owner's stake.

activities.anchor: not because accountants are tidy, but because it could not be otherwise
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the equation and its turn-around
activities.name: acEquationCloze

config.text: The accounting equation reads %%0%% = liabilities + capital — every asset was paid for by an outsider or by the owner. Turned around, capital = assets %%1%% liabilities, the number accountants call net assets.
config.hint: Only two somehows exist: outsiders supplied the money, or the owner did.

activities.anchor: deliberately independent for exactly this reason
activities.caption: true or false — profit vs cash
activities.name: acCashJudge

statements.s: A profitable business can run out of cash.
statements.why: Sales on credit, or cash locked in inventory and machines that have not turned back into cash yet.

statements.s: Profit measures performance over a period; cash measures a balance at a moment.
statements.why: The video and the photograph again — the two readouts in the lab are deliberately independent.

statements.s: Money the owner withdraws for personal use is an expense of the business.
statements.why: Drawings come out of the owner's stake — the owner is not 'costing' the firm.

statements.s: A loss-making business is always short of cash.
statements.why: Fresh capital or asset sales can leave a loss-maker flush with cash.

activities.anchor: has its own lesson later in this course
activities.caption: bet first — the dual effect on one sale
activities.name: acDualPredict

config.q: You sell goods for 800 dollars in cash that cost you 500 dollars. Which three things happen?
choices: Cash +800 only — profit arrives when the owner withdraws it
config.why: The dual effect: inventory falls, cash rises, and the 300-dollar difference is profit — which belongs to the owner, so capital rises. Every transaction touches at least two things.

activities.caption: call the magnitude — the fruit stall's margin
activities.name: acMarginEstimate

config.prompt: Profit is 13,000 dollars on sales of 50,000 dollars. Roughly what is the profit margin, in per cent?
config.why: 13,000 ÷ 50,000 = 26 per cent — a margin only means something against a benchmark: grocery chains run single digits on enormous turnover; software firms run huge margins on modest capital.
config.context: The monitoring-progress purpose from earlier, come back around.
